q: A Vinho Verde smelling emphatically of bay laurel, orange blossom and lime takes its name from that scent. Which variety?
exp: Loureiro is named for the laurel and is the most aromatic of the region's workhorse whites, at its best around the Lima valley. Trajadura lends body and low acid to a blend, while Avesso needs the warmer inland sites of Baiao.

q: In the Minho a black grape gives an inky, sharply acidic red that locals drink from white ceramic bowls. Which variety?
exp: Vinhao has coloured pulp as well as coloured skin, so the wine stains the bowl it is poured into. It is bracing and low in alcohol, made for grilled sardines and cured pork rather than for export.

q: One white grape appears in Minho blends under the local name Pederna, while Bucelas builds its entire reputation on it. Which grape?
exp: Arinto holds its acidity even in real heat, which is why it travels the length of the country and turns up in Alentejo blends as well. Pederna is simply its Minho name.

q: Boundary stones planted in the years after 1756, under the Marquis of Pombal, still stand among the vines above the river. What did they establish?
opts: The land border between Portugal and Spain
A tax boundary with no connection to wine
One of the first demarcated wine regions
The first cooperative winery in Europe
exp: Pombal's chartered company of 1756 fixed the limits of the region, graded the vineyards and controlled prices, largely to stop the adulteration of wine sold to the British trade. That combination of a fixed boundary and enforced rules puts it among the earliest regulated wine regions anywhere. The marcos pombalinos, cut and set out over the years that followed, are still in the ground.

q: Vines on the steepest Douro slopes survive summers with almost no rain by rooting metres down through fractured rock. Which rock?
exp: Schist splits into near-vertical plates, so roots follow the fissures down to moisture the surface lost months earlier. Granite appears at the region's margins but does not fracture the same way, and roots cannot exploit it as deeply.

q: Moving upstream from Mesao Frio toward the Spanish border, in what order do the three Douro sub-regions appear?
opts: Cima Corgo, then Baixo Corgo, then Douro Superior
Baixo Corgo, then Cima Corgo, then Douro Superior
Douro Superior, then Cima Corgo, then Baixo Corgo
Baixo Corgo, then Douro Superior, then Cima Corgo
exp: The Corgo is a tributary joining at Regua, and the two names mean below and above it. Rainfall drops and heat climbs steadily eastward, so the Douro Superior is the hottest and the least densely planted of the three.

q: Narrow ledges walled in dry schist, holding one or two rows of vines apiece, climb the oldest Douro slopes. What are they called?
exp: Socalcos were built by hand over centuries and cannot take a tractor, so everything on them is still done by people and mules. Patamares, the bulldozed earth-banked terraces of the 1970s onward, replaced them wherever mechanisation mattered more than history.

q: On slopes gentle enough to allow it, Douro growers now plant rows running straight up and down the hill instead of across it. What does that buy?
opts: A tractor can work the rows
The fruit ripens a full month earlier
exp: Vinha ao alto removes the terrace entirely, so a tractor can climb the rows instead of crawling along ledges, and it fits more vines on the same ground. It only works below roughly a thirty percent gradient, and it needs careful cover cropping, because water running downhill takes soil with it.

q: Every Douro vineyard is scored on altitude, gradient, soil, yield and grape mix, and the letter grade it earns controls one thing specifically. What?
opts: Whether the estate is allowed to bottle unfortified wine
The number of vines permitted per hectare
How much of its must may be fortified into Port each year
The price its bottles may be sold for
exp: The cadastro grades run from A to F, and the annual beneficio allocates fortification rights accordingly. Whatever is not turned into Port stays available for unfortified Douro wine.

q: Unfortified red from the Douro was long dismissed as a by-product until a wine first made in 1952 changed the argument. Which wine?
exp: Fernando Nicolau de Almeida modelled it on Bordeaux, hauling ice up from the coast to cool the ferment. It is declared only in years judged worthy, and it opened the road to the Douro DOC granted three decades later.

q: Ripening late and cropping more generously than Touriga Nacional, which Douro variety supplies perfume and supple fruit to a blend?
exp: Budding and ripening late protects Touriga Franca from spring frost and suits the hottest sites in the valley. It gives floral lift and softer tannin where Touriga Nacional gives density and structure.

q: White wine from the Douro has turned serious in the last generation, grown high up or on slopes facing away from the sun. Which grapes carry it?
opts: Antao Vaz, Roupeiro, Perrum and Diagalves
Viosinho, Rabigato, Gouveio and Codega do Larinho
exp: Rabigato brings the acidity, Viosinho the body and Gouveio the citrus, the last being the grape Madeira calls Verdelho. Altitude does most of the work, since the best white parcels sit six hundred metres up or on north-facing schist where the fruit never bakes.

q: Ringed by the Serra do Caramulo, the Serra da Nave and the Serra da Estrela, one region grows vines in clearings among pine forest, most of them four to five hundred metres up and some as high as eight hundred. Which?
exp: The mountains take the edge off the Atlantic from the west and the Spanish meseta from the east, giving a long, temperate growing season. Granite sand underfoot and pine on every horizon are the region's signature.

q: Underneath the Dao's vineyards lies a poor, free-draining, acidic sand weathered from one bedrock. Which?
exp: Granitic sand gives low vigour and small crops, and it is much of why Dao reds feel firmer and more mineral than the riper, softer reds of the southern plains. Schist appears only in patches at the edges.

q: For decades Dao growers were obliged by law to sell their fruit to the local cooperative, and private houses could buy only finished wine. What did that produce?
opts: Exceptionally consistent quality across every producer
A ban on estate bottling that remains in force today
Dull, uniform wine and a damaged reputation
A rapid rise in single-vineyard bottlings
exp: Everyone's fruit went into the same vats and the wine was then held far too long in old wood, which is why the reds of that era taste dried out and tannic rather than thin. The monopoly held from the Salazar era until the late 1980s, when Portugal's entry into the European Community swept it away, and estate bottling followed.

q: One Portuguese white grape carries enough structure and acidity to be barrel-fermented and cellared for a decade, and it belongs to the Dao. Which?
exp: Encruzado is unusually restrained in aroma for a Portuguese white, which is exactly why it takes oak and time without being smothered. Comparisons with white Burgundy are made often and are not absurd.
